title: Model-level synthetic-flux control of hyperchaos order and matched-resource sensing in dissipative optomechanics
authors: Stella Rolande Mbokop Tchounda, Carolle Tchodimou, Philippe Djorwe, Sifeu Takougang Kingni, Serge Guy Nana Engo
abstract:
Within a normalised six-dimensional model of dissipative optomechanics (one cavity + two mechanical resonators), a synthetic-flux phase $Φ_{m syn}$ selects the \emph{order} of a drive- and coupling-gated hyperchaos transition---up to four simultaneously unstable Lyapunov directions, beyond any reported single-mode benchmark---while the same matched-resource force-sensing protocol yields no flux-induced enhancement on the chaotic attractor. Building on the topology of Muthukumar \emph{et al.}~[PR Applied 	extbf{24}, 014053 (2025)], a phase-consistent Floquet--Lyapunov protocol (cross-checked by monodromy multipliers, dissipative volume balance and a 180-run three-seed audit) localises a Neimark--Sacker bifurcation at $E^{*}=
um{1.060}$ ($θ=0$). At a weakly coupled reference the matched Fisher gain reaches at most $
um{1.32}	imes$ (flux-off) and $
um{1.16}	imes$ (single-mode), with Monte-Carlo median $
um{1.039}	imes$ (90\,\% CI $[
um{1.025},
um{1.053}]$); on the chaotic attractor the identical protocol returns a null result ($\mathcal{G}_{A/B}=
um{1.039}\pm
um{0.014}$). Truncated-Fock and truncated-Wigner checks support the mean-field description at selected points. Both the hyperchaos classification and the sensing result remain strictly model-level: the strong-coupling sector explored here lies $
um{2542}	imes$ beyond anchored silicon optomechanical couplings. Closing that gap requires a measured inter-resonator hopping $J_m$ and fixed bath temperatures.
summary: This work models a complex dissipative optomechanical system to demonstrate that a synthetic-flux phase can precisely control the degree of hyperchaos. While the control of chaos is robustly shown, the study concludes that this flux control does not translate into a measurable enhancement for force sensing on the chaotic attractor, suggesting limitations in the sensing protocol.
main_problem: The study investigates the control of hyperchaos order and the performance of matched-resource sensing in a dissipative optomechanical system using a synthetic-flux phase.
main_result: The synthetic-flux phase successfully controls the hyperchaos order up to four unstable Lyapunov directions, but the matched-resource sensing protocol yields no flux-induced enhancement on the chaotic attractor.
method: The analysis employs advanced dynamical systems diagnostics, including calculating the full Lyapunov spectrum, analyzing the Poincaré map via monodromy multipliers, and evaluating the matched Fisher information.
model_or_system: The system is a dissipative optomechanical model comprising one cavity and two mechanical resonators, analyzed using semiclassical equations of motion derived from a Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Hyperchaos order (number of positive Lyapunov exponents), Matched Fisher gain, Neimark-Sacker bifurcation points, and Lyapunov exponents.
important_parameters: Synthetic-flux phase ($\Phi_{syn}$), Drive amplitude ($E$), Coupling strengths ($g_1, g_2$), and damping rates ($\kappa, \gamma$).
main_assumptions: The strong-coupling regime explored is highly idealized and far beyond current experimental anchors; the analysis relies on consistency checks across multiple diagnostic tools.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the validation of consistency metrics (QR exponents), the dependence of Lyapunov exponents on drive amplitude and flux phase, and the correlation dimension of the attractor.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the model, detailing the consistency checks (Lyapunov-Floquet), demonstrating flux control over hyperchaos order, and finally analyzing the sensing gain on the resulting chaotic attractor.
why_interesting: It combines advanced nonlinear dynamics (hyperchaos control) with quantum measurement theory (Fisher information) within the context of cavity optomechanics, providing a rigorous, albeit model-level, testbed for quantum control.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Long-window validation across nine synthetic-flux phases and three independent initial conditions per phase. (a) The largest QR exponents remain negative at every sampled phase. (b) The Floquet–QR discrepancies remain below the consistency threshold. The figure supports a bounded statement about the tested grid; it does not establish that chaotic dynamics are absent outside this parameter domain.

Figure 2: Full-spectrum transition map at weak coupling. (a) All six Lyapunov exponents versus the synthetic-flux phase at drive E = 0.2; the two cavity- dominated exponents (lower panel, near −κ/2 ≈−0.5) and the four mechani- cal exponents (upper panel, near −γ/2 ≈−0.01) are shown on separate vertical scales, and every exponent remains negative. (b) Largest (most marginal) ex- ponent versus drive amplitude, with the phase-to-phase spread shaded; it stays negative across E ∈[0.2, 8.0]. (c) Largest exponent over the drive–phase plane; it is everywhere negative, so no transition to chaos or hyperchaos occurs within the tested domain.

Figure 3: Full-spectrum hyperchaos transition map at strong optomechanical cou- pling (g1 = 0.3, g2 = 0.27, γ1,2 = 0.02, ∆= −ωm; model-level parameters lying ∼2500× beyond silicon anchors). (a) All six Lyapunov exponents versus the synthetic-flux phase at drive E = 4.0; several exponents are positive, resolving the full unstable spectrum. (b) Hyperchaos order (number of exponents above the fixed strong threshold 1 × 10−3) versus phase at E = 0.2, 4.0 and 8.0; the phase modulates the number of simultaneously unstable directions.
